section.title: By Grace Through Faith
section.sectionRationale: Here the great blessings of chapter one come down to earth in the story of every believer. Paul describes the human condition in the starkest terms, dead in sin, enslaved to the world, the devil, and the flesh, and children of wrath, and then interrupts it with two of the most glorious words in Scripture: but God. Salvation is shown to be entirely God's gift of grace, received through faith, producing a people created for good works. This is the gospel in miniature.
section.thesis: We were spiritually dead, enslaved, and under wrath, but God, rich in mercy and great in love, made us alive with Christ, raised us, and seated us with Him, saving us by grace through faith as His own gift, so that no one can boast, and creating us anew in Christ for the good works He prepared beforehand.
section.frameNote: Three movements: our former state, dead in trespasses and by nature children of wrath; the great reversal, but God, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ; and the summary, saved by grace through faith, God's gift, His workmanship created for good works.

units.label: Dead in sin
units.note: the world, the devil, and the flesh

verses.text: And you were {{nekros|dead}} in your trespasses and sins,
in which you used to walk when you conformed to the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience.
All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath.

units.label: But God, rich in mercy, made us alive

verses.text: But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy,
made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by {{charis|grace}} you have been saved!
And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus,
in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace, demonstrated by His kindness to us in Christ Jesus.

units.label: Saved by grace through faith, created for good works

verses.text: For it is by grace you have been {{sozo|saved}} through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the {{doron|gift}} of God,
not by works, so that no one can boast.
For we are God's {{poiema|workmanship}}, {{ktizo|created}} in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.

nekros.gloss: Dead, a corpse, without life. Paul does not say we were merely sick or weak in sin but dead in trespasses and sins, spiritually lifeless and unable to raise ourselves. This diagnosis is the dark backdrop against which grace shines: only the God who raises the dead can save people in such a state.

charis.gloss: Grace, free and unearned favor, a gift given with no thought of repayment. It is the great keyword of the passage, breaking in with by grace you have been saved. Grace is God's kindness shown to those who deserve wrath, and Paul insists it is the whole ground of salvation, ruling out any human boast.

sozo.gloss: To save, rescue, deliver, and make whole. Notably Paul uses the perfect tense, you have been saved, marking salvation as an accomplished reality with lasting effect, not a hope still hanging in the balance. The rescue is from death, wrath, and bondage into life with Christ.

doron.gloss: A gift, something freely given. Salvation is the gift of God, not a wage earned or a prize won. The word underlines that the whole of this rescue, from first to last, originates in God's generosity and is received with empty hands, leaving no room for pride.

poiema.gloss: That which is made, a work or masterpiece, from which the English word poem derives. Believers are God's own handiwork, crafted by Him. The word frames the Christian life as God's creative project: we do not make ourselves, we are made new by the Maker for a purpose He has set.

ktizo.gloss: To create, the verb used for God's original act of creation. To be created in Christ Jesus is to be made new, a fresh act of divine creation bringing life where there was death. The same power that made the world remakes the believer for the good works God has prepared in advance.

basic.context: Paul now tells the story of every Christian. We began dead in our sins, walking in step with the world, following the devil, driven by our own cravings, and standing under God's wrath by nature. Then come the two greatest words: but God. Because of His great love and rich mercy, God made us alive with Christ, raised us, and seated us with Him. Salvation is by grace through faith, entirely God's gift, so that no one can boast, and we are His new creation, made for good works He planned long ago.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage moves in three beats: our hopeless condition, God's merciful intervention, and the nature of the salvation He gives. The turning point is the phrase but God in verse 4. Read it as a rescue story in which the rescued contribute nothing but the deadness that needed reviving. The good works of verse 10 are the goal and result of salvation, never its cause.
basic.originalLanguages: We were nekros, dead, in trespasses and sins, lifeless and helpless. But God, rich in mercy, saved us by charis, grace, unearned favor. Paul says you have been sozo, saved, an accomplished rescue that stands. Salvation is the doron, the gift, of God, not of works. And we are His poiema, His workmanship or masterpiece, ktizo, created anew, in Christ Jesus for good works.
basic.typology: Being made alive, raised, and seated with Christ ties the believer's story to Christ's own death, resurrection, and enthronement, so that His history becomes ours. Creation in Christ echoes the first creation in Genesis, when God made humanity and called it good; now, in Christ, God performs a new creation, bringing life out of the death sin had caused.
basic.christ: Everything happens with Christ and in Christ: we are made alive with Him, raised with Him, and seated with Him in the heavenly realms. His resurrection and enthronement, described in chapter one, are shared with all who are joined to Him. Christ is the sphere of the new creation, the one in whom the dead are made alive and remade for good works.
basic.god: God is the hero of this passage: rich in mercy, great in love, and lavish in grace. He acts while we are still dead, moved by nothing outside Himself but His own love. His purpose reaches into the coming ages, that He might display the surpassing riches of His grace forever. He is a God who saves the helpless and gets all the glory.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 5 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, and that God shows His love to the ungodly. Colossians 2 speaks of being made alive together with Christ, forgiven all our trespasses. Titus 3 declares that God saved us not by works but according to His mercy.
basic.oneStory: This is the gospel in miniature, the movement of the whole Bible from death to life. The fall left humanity dead in sin and under wrath, but God's rescuing love, promised from Genesis onward, breaks in with but God. The new creation begun here points to the day when all things are made new, a people raised with Christ and walking in the good works their Maker prepared.

context.literary:
Ephesians 2:1 to 10 is, like the passages on each side of it, one long Greek sentence in the first seven verses, and its shape is a pivot. Verses 1 to 3 are a description with no main verb in sight: 'you were dead,' 'we all lived,' 'we were by nature children of wrath.' The grammar itself is stuck, waiting for a verb to rescue it. The main verb arrives in verse 5, 'made alive,' and it is followed immediately by two more verbs of the same family, 'raised' and 'seated,' in verse 6. The structure mirrors the message: a long silence of death, then God acts.

The passage is built on three contrasts. The first is between 'you' in verses 1 and 2 and 'we all' in verse 3. Paul begins by speaking to the Gentile readers and then includes himself and his fellow Jews, so that the verdict falls on both. The second is between 'were' and 'but God.' The third, in verses 8 to 10, is between what comes 'from yourselves' and what is 'the gift of God,' between 'works' and 'workmanship.' Notice also that the passage is bracketed by walking. In verse 2 they 'used to walk' in trespasses; in verse 10 God has prepared good works for them to walk in. The same verb stands at either end and marks the change of direction.

The three 'with' verbs, made alive with, raised with and seated with, are all compounds beginning with the Greek preposition for 'together with.' The effect is to say that the believer's story is joined to Christ's at every point. The passage then looks forward in verse 7, 'in the coming ages,' before landing in verses 8 to 10 in the plainest summary of the gospel anywhere in Paul.
context.historical:
The Ephesian church was made of Gentiles and Jews, and the first three verses speak to both. The phrases 'the ways of this world' and 'the ruler of the power of the air' reflect a world in which people believed the air between earth and heaven was filled with spiritual beings. Greek and Roman religion, and the magic that thrived in Ephesus, assumed this. Paul agrees that there is a spiritual ruler at work but tells believers that this ruler's grip was broken.

Within the Jewish world, the phrase 'by nature children of wrath' stated something Jews would readily accept of Gentiles but find hard to accept of themselves. Many Jews believed that the covenant and the law marked them as secure, and the opponents Paul fights elsewhere insisted on works of the law. Putting 'all of us' under the same verdict, so that the Jewish Christian Paul is included in 'children of wrath,' strips away any claim that Jews begin from a better position. The same levelling runs through Romans 3:9 and 3:23.

The social background of 'the coming ages' and 'display' also matters. In a world of patrons, benefactors were known for displaying their generosity publicly, with monuments and inscriptions. Paul says God displays the surpassing riches of His grace to the ages by His kindness to the undeserving, so the ones saved become, as it were, the gallery. The language of grace in the first century also belonged to patronage, where a gift created obligations. Paul takes the vocabulary and says that this gift can never be repaid, and the proper response is not an attempt to settle accounts but a life of good works that flow from it.
context.canonical:
The picture of the dead being given life is a major theme of the Old Testament. In Ezekiel 37 a valley of dry bones is told to hear the word of the LORD and they live, as God says 'I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life.' The restoration of Israel is spoken of as resurrection. Paul reads that promise as being fulfilled in the individual believer joined to the risen Christ. Hosea 6:2 and Isaiah 26:19 point the same way.

The description of the human condition recalls the whole witness of Scripture. Genesis 6:5 and Psalm 51:5 speak of a human heart evil from early on, Isaiah 64:6 of righteous acts like filthy rags, and Romans 3:23 of all having sinned. The 'wrath' of verse 3 matches Romans 1:18, where the wrath of God is revealed against all ungodliness, and Jesus is the one who delivers from the coming wrath, 1 Thessalonians 1:10.

The remedy is the grace and mercy of God, found in Exodus 34:6, where the LORD describes Himself as compassionate and gracious. Salvation by grace through faith is taught in Genesis 15:6, where Abraham believed and it was credited to him as righteousness, which Paul quotes in Romans 4:3. Titus 3:5, 'He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy,' is a close sister passage, and Romans 3:21 to 28 states the same doctrine more fully. Romans 11:6 says plainly that grace and works exclude each other.

Verse 10 draws on creation language. The word 'created' is the vocabulary of Genesis 1, and the good works prepared beforehand recall Isaiah 26:12, 'all that we have accomplished You have done for us.' James 2:17 and 18 then shows that real faith produces works, which is the other side of Ephesians 2:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to move people from pride to praise. Verses 1 to 3 destroy the idea that anyone brings anything to salvation except the need for it. Verses 4 to 7 put the whole initiative in God, and verses 8 to 10 draw the conclusion that boasting is excluded. His readers are Gentiles who might think their entry into the people of God was a favour they had earned by faith, and Jews who might think their heritage mattered. Both are told the same thing: all of it is gift.

He also wants to protect against a misreading. Having said that works do not save, he immediately says that works are what we are saved for. He is not offering a cheap grace in which nothing is asked of us, nor a hard grace that must be worked up to. He wants a life that grows out of the gift, one in which people walk in the good works God prepared for them. In other words he wants gratitude to show up as a way of life.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage is almost entirely description, a description of what we were, what God did, and what we now are. It contains very few commands, and none in the usual sense. Even the last verse, about good works, is phrased as a description of God's purpose, 'which God prepared in advance as our way of life.' Applying it correctly means first receiving the description as a gift, since the passage is meant to be believed before anything is done.

The verses cannot be turned into a method for earning salvation or measuring someone else's. They also should not be read as saying that all people are equally wicked in every act or that no unbeliever can do any good, since Paul's claim is about our standing before God and our spiritual inability to make ourselves alive. What does follow directly is that boasting is excluded, that pastors and teachers should preach grace as a gift, and that believers should expect their lives to be marked by good works as the outflow, not the root, of their salvation.

debates.question: What does 'this' refer to in 'this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God'?

views.label: The whole of salvation by grace through faith
views.case: In Greek, the word for 'this' is neuter, while 'grace' and 'faith' are both feminine, so it does not match either word. It most naturally refers to the whole event described by the clause, being saved by grace through faith. This reading is held by many commentators, and it fits the context, where the emphasis is on God's gift of the entire thing.

views.label: Faith itself is the gift
views.case: Faith is the nearest feminine noun, and the thought that even faith is given matches Philippians 1:29, 'it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him,' and John 6:44. Augustine and many Reformers read it this way, to leave no corner for self-credit.

views.label: Grace is the gift
views.case: Grace is the main subject of verses 5 to 7. The neuter 'this' can point back to the concept of grace as a gift, and a neuter pronoun that refers to a feminine idea is not unusual.

debates.bearing: All three land on the same point, that nothing in salvation originates in us. The first reading fits the grammar best; the second is supported by other texts and in any case true. The practical result is that Paul closes every door to boasting.

debates.question: What is meant by 'children of wrath by nature'?

views.label: Inherited fallen nature
views.case: 'By nature' points to what we are from birth, matching Psalm 51:5 and Romans 5:12 to 19, where all share Adam's condition. Augustine and the Reformers took this as a statement of original sin, so people are born under wrath and spiritually dead.

views.label: Settled character formed by habit
views.case: Some take 'by nature' as meaning 'truly, in actuality,' and read the clause as describing people who have become what they are through practice, as 'fulfilling the cravings of our flesh' describes. On this reading the verse describes how things stand with us, without claiming anything about birth.

debates.bearing: The point of the passage is the universal need, 'all of us,' and the universal rescue. It is clear that no one is exempt and no one can save themselves. Paul's point does not turn on settling how the condition passes on.

study.originalLanguages:
This passage rewards a close look at its grammar, which does a good deal of the teaching.

The first thing to see is the phrase 'trespasses and sins' in verse 1. Paul uses two words for wrongdoing. Paraptoma suggests a slip or a falling away, a false step, and hamartia is the more general word for missing the mark or sin as a power. The two together cover both individual acts and the underlying condition. The picture is of a person living inside a graveyard of their own making.

Second, the word 'walk' in verse 2 is peripateo, a standard Hebrew style metaphor for the pattern of a whole life, and it recurs in the letter, at 2:10, 4:1, 5:2, 5:8 and 5:15. The 'age of this world,' as the Greek has it, uses aion, a stretch of time with a character of its own, as in Galatians 1:4, 'the present evil age.' The 'ruler of the power of the air' places a hostile ruler in the unseen realm, and Paul says his influence is ongoing.

Third, the three compound verbs of verses 5 and 6. The Greek sunezoopoiesen, sunegeiren and sunekathisen each begin with sun, 'together with.' Made alive with, raised with, seated with. The first and second compounds are paralleled in Colossians 2:13 and 2:12, while the third is distinctive to Ephesians. The verbs are in the aorist, treating these as completed events, even the seating in heavenly places, which is future in ordinary experience. Paul's point is that in Christ the future has been brought forward.

Fourth, the phrase 'you have been saved' is a periphrastic perfect, with a participle and the verb 'to be.' This describes a completed state that continues, and Paul uses it in both verses 5 and 8. It is the basis for the confidence that salvation is not a repeated process.

Fifth, the word for 'display' in verse 7 is built on a root meaning to show, to point out, used for a demonstration that others can see, and the word for 'kindness' is chrestotes, a gentle and generous goodness, used of God in Romans 2:4 and Titus 3:4. The two together say that God's kindness is not private but exhibited.

Finally, in verse 10, poiema, 'workmanship,' is the word from which we get poem and means something made, a work of art. It appears in the New Testament only here and in Romans 1:20, where it is used of creation as God's handiwork. The verb 'prepared in advance' means to make ready beforehand, and the clause says that we should walk in the works. The 'works' are not our invention; they are laid out for us.

typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel 37 pictures Israel as dry bones in exile, brought to life by the word and the breath of God. Paul uses the same imagery, with believers dead and made alive by God's act alone, not by anything the bones could do. In Christ the vision becomes personal: Colossians 2:13 says 'God made you alive with Christ.' The type falls short because Ezekiel's vision was a promise about a nation's restoration, while Ephesians describes the actual raising of persons, joined to Christ's own resurrection, Romans 6:4.

Israel was a people in bondage who did nothing to deserve freedom, and the LORD brought them out for love and for His oath, Deuteronomy 7:8. In Ephesians 2:2 and 2:3 believers are described as enslaved to a ruler, to flesh and to the world, and rescued by God. The exodus gave a pattern of salvation as pure grace, for the people simply stood and watched, Exodus 14:13. It falls short in that the exodus freed from a human tyrant, while this rescue frees from sin and the powers behind it.

Genesis 1 pictures God creating by His word from darkness and void. The Ephesians were 'created in Christ Jesus' in verse 10, and 2 Corinthians 4:6 says God, who said 'Let light shine out of darkness,' made His light shine in our hearts. The pattern is that salvation is a creation, an act that does not depend on material already present. It is incomplete until the resurrection of the body and the renewal of the earth, Romans 8:23.

The Old Testament knew of those who stood before the LORD, but only a king was seated at His right hand, Psalm 110:1. Paul says believers are seated with Christ, sharing His position by union. Colossians 3:1 and Revelation 3:21 develop the thought, with believers promised a place on His throne. It is the shadow of royal rule, brought to the whole people, and it is not complete in experience until Christ's rule is visibly total, 1 Corinthians 15:25.

study.christ:
This passage speaks of God's act 'in Christ Jesus,' and the angles are distinct.

First, Christ is the one with whom we are made alive. The preposition 'with' puts His history and ours side by side. He died, and we were dead; He was raised, and we are made alive; He was seated, and we are seated. Colossians 2:12 and 13 says the same, that believers were buried with Him and raised with Him. Romans 6:4 says we were buried with Him in baptism so as to walk in newness of life. The first answer to 'How are people saved?' is 'by being joined to the person who went through death for them.'

Second, Christ is the place of grace. The grace of verses 5 to 8 is not given in the air. It is given 'in Christ Jesus' in verse 7 and verse 10, and it is demonstrated in kindness 'to us in Christ Jesus.' Titus 3:4 to 7 says God's kindness and love appeared, and that He saved us through Jesus Christ our Savior. Romans 3:24 says we are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

Third, Christ is the answer to the verdict of verse 3. Wrath was the condition of verse 3, and 1 Thessalonians 1:10 says that Jesus is the one who delivers us from the coming wrath. The great love of verse 4 was expressed concretely, as Romans 5:8 says, 'while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.' The 'But God' of verse 4 is not a bare fact; it is the cross and the resurrection.

Fourth, Christ is the one who makes the new creation. Verse 10 says that we are created in Christ Jesus. 2 Corinthians 5:17 says that anyone in Christ is a new creation, and Colossians 1:15 to 18 shows Him as the one through whom the first creation came and the firstborn of the new. Ephesians 4:24 says we put on the new self created to be like God.

Fifth, Christ is the pattern of the good works that were prepared. He walked in the works the Father gave Him to do, John 5:36, and He is the one into whom the believer grows, Ephesians 4:15. The works of verse 10 are the works of Christ's body, done by His Spirit.

A caution against forced allegory: the 'ruler of the power of the air' is not a code for any person, and the 'coming ages' do not hide a timetable. The point is that Christ is the content and the cause of our salvation, which Paul states plainly.
study.god:
The passage gives a vivid picture of God, and the most important feature is the contrast between what we were and what God is.

First, God is rich in mercy. The word 'rich' is typical of Paul, who says elsewhere 'the riches of His grace,' Ephesians 1:7, and 'the riches of His kindness,' Romans 2:4. Mercy is God's response to misery, and the passage says He has a store of it. The misery described is complete, death, bondage, wrath, so the mercy is of the same extent. Exodus 34:6 describes the LORD as compassionate and gracious, and this passage shows that character acted out.

Second, God is moved by love and not by anything in us. 'Because of His great love for us' is placed before any mention of human response. John 3:16 says that He so loved the world that He gave, and 1 John 4:10 says that love consists not in our loving God but in His loving us. The doctrine of God here is that He is the source of love and does not need to be won over.

Third, God is the giver of life. The passage says He made us alive, which only God can do. He is the Creator who spoke the first world into being and raised the Son from the dead. There is no cooperation from the dead, so salvation shows His power. Ezekiel 37:5 puts the words in His mouth, 'I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life.'

Fourth, God is just and gracious at once. The wrath of verse 3 is real, and the grace of verse 5 does not ignore it, because the rescue passes through Christ's death. Romans 3:25 and 26 says God presented Christ as an atoning sacrifice so as to be just and to justify. The passage holds together a God who is angry at sin and a God who is overflowing with love, and says that the two meet at the cross.

Fifth, God is a planner of good. The works of verse 10 were 'prepared in advance,' which says that God's plan includes not just our rescue but the shape of our lives afterwards. Philippians 2:13 says it is God who works in us to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose. The obedience of the believer is a result of God's work, and so there is no ground for pride in it either.

Sixth, God is a God who displays. He saves so that 'in the coming ages' He might show the riches of His grace. The purpose is His glory, in keeping with the first chapter's refrain. The universe is meant to see what kind of God He is by looking at the rescued.

The response for worship is gratitude that is humble and glad. There is nothing here to be proud of, and everything to praise.

crossReferences.note: The valley of dry bones, brought to life by the word and breath of the LORD. It is the Old Testament picture of life given to the dead by God alone, and it stands behind Paul's 'made alive.' It also shows that the dead contribute nothing but their need.

'You were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God... God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our trespasses.' It is the nearest parallel to verses 5 and 6, and links being made alive to forgiveness.

'He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy,' through the Spirit, so that we become heirs. It states the same doctrine of mercy over works and ends in the same hope of inheritance.

Righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ, and all are justified freely by His grace, so that boasting is excluded. It is the full argument for the conclusion Paul draws in verses 8 and 9.

'If it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.' It states the logic that grace and works cannot be mixed as the ground of salvation, which is the principle behind verse 9.

'It has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him.' It supports the reading that even believing is a gift, bearing on 'this is not from yourselves.'
Christ died for the ungodly while we were weak, enemies and sinners. It is the concrete display of 'because of His great love for us' in verse 4, and the demonstration of mercy for the undeserving.

'Faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.' It does not contradict Paul but shows the other side of verse 10, that real faith produces works, which Paul himself says God prepared for us.

The power that raised Christ and seated Him at God's right hand is the same power that now raises believers. It connects the prayer of chapter 1 with the experience described here, and the 'seated' language is shared.
'All our righteous acts are like filthy rags.' It supports the verdict of verses 1 to 3 and the exclusion of works in verse 9, because even the best of our deeds cannot bring us to life.

study.oneStory:
Ephesians 2:1 to 10 is the whole Bible's story in ten verses. Creation is implied in the word 'created,' the fall is in the opening verses of death, bondage and wrath, redemption is the 'But God' that turns the story, and new creation is in the verbs of being raised and seated and the promise of the coming ages.

What does it answer from before? It answers the question that the Old Testament asks again and again, 'Can these bones live?' Israel in exile was dead in everything but name, and the prophets promised that God would breathe life into them. It also answers the problem of how a holy God can show mercy to rebels. Genesis 3 left humanity under a sentence of death. The law then showed more clearly how deep the problem went, Romans 5:20, and the prophets kept announcing that God Himself would act. Ephesians 2 says He has.

What does it set up? Immediately, verses 11 to 22, where those who were far off are brought near and Jew and Gentile become one new man and a holy temple. The same grace which saves individuals gathers a people. It also sets up chapters 4 to 6, the walk in good works, where those who were dead and walked in trespasses now walk in love and light. And it sets up the continuing story of the church, which is the display of grace 'in the coming ages.'

How does it end? In the new creation. The believer is already raised and seated, but the full inheritance is still to come. Revelation 21:5 has the voice from the throne say, 'Behold, I make all things new,' and 1 Corinthians 15:42 to 44 describes the body sown in perishability and raised in imperishability. The 'coming ages' of verse 7 are the long future in which God shows what His grace has done, with the rescued as the proof. The story that started with a good creation and a fall ends with a people made alive, seated with their King, and the universe looking on to see how kind God has been.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe our condition before God's saving work?

options.text: Dead in trespasses and sins, enslaved and by nature children of wrath.
options.note: Verses 1 to 3 describe spiritual death, bondage, and wrath.

options.text: Basically healthy but needing a little improvement.
options.note: Paul says we were dead, not merely in need of self-help.

options.text: Weak and struggling, but able to save ourselves with effort.
options.note: The dead cannot revive themselves; only God can make them alive.

options.text: Already reconciled to God apart from Christ.
options.note: We were under wrath and dead in sin until God intervened.

quiz.q: What are the pivotal words that turn the passage in verse 4?

options.text: But God, who is rich in mercy.
options.note: The great reversal hinges on God's merciful intervention.

options.text: But we, who tried our best.
options.note: The turn is God's action, not human effort.

options.text: But the law, which set us free.
options.note: It is God's mercy, not the law, that rescues.

options.text: But time, which healed our wounds.
options.note: Deliverance comes from God's mercy, not the passing of time.

quiz.q: On what basis are we saved, according to verse 8?

options.text: By grace, through faith, as the gift of God.
options.note: Salvation is grace received by faith, God's gift from start to finish.

options.text: By grace plus our own meritorious works.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly excludes works, so no one can boast.

options.text: By our sincerity and religious devotion.
options.note: It is God's gift, not from ourselves.

options.text: By keeping the law perfectly.
options.note: Salvation is not by works but by grace through faith.

quiz.q: Why does Paul stress that salvation is not by works?

options.text: So that no one can boast; all glory belongs to God.
options.note: Verse 9 excludes boasting because salvation is God's gift.

options.text: So that good works no longer matter at all.
options.note: Works still matter as the goal of salvation, verse 10, just not its ground.

options.text: So that we can feel superior to those who work.
options.note: The point is humility before God, not pride over others.

options.text: Because human effort earns a share of the credit.
options.note: The whole aim is that no one can boast; God gets the glory.

quiz.q: What does it mean that we are God's workmanship?

options.text: We are His handiwork, created anew in Christ for good works.
options.note: Verse 10 calls us God's poiema, created in Christ for the works He prepared.

options.text: We craft ourselves into better people by our own design.
options.note: We are made by God, not self-made.

options.text: We are a finished project with nothing more to live for.
options.note: We are created for good works, a purpose God has prepared.

options.text: We are saved in order to earn our standing by works.
options.note: Good works are the result of salvation, not its price.

quiz.q: How do the good works of verse 10 relate to salvation?

options.text: They are the result and goal of salvation, prepared by God beforehand.
options.note: We are created in Christ for good works God prepared in advance.

options.text: They are the price we pay to be saved.
options.note: Salvation is a gift, not by works; the works follow it.

options.text: They are optional extras with no real place in the Christian life.
options.note: They are the very purpose for which we were created in Christ.

options.text: They earn a higher rank of salvation over time.
options.note: Works flow from grace as its fruit, not as a way to climb higher.

questions: Paul says we were dead in sin, not merely weak. How does seeing salvation as being raised from death, rather than helped along, change the way you view God's grace to you?
The passage turns on two words, but God. Where in your life do you need to hear that but God interrupt a story that felt hopeless?
Salvation is a gift, not a wage, so that no one can boast. Where are you still tempted to think God accepts you because of what you do rather than because of His grace?
You are seated with Christ in the heavenly realms even now. How does sharing in His exaltation change the way you face today's struggles and fears?
You are God's workmanship, created for good works He prepared in advance. How does knowing your good works are planned by God free you to serve without pressure to earn His love?

translationNotes.note: Children of wrath renders a Hebrew style idiom meaning those who are objects of wrath by nature, describing our standing under God's just judgment apart from grace, not that God delights in anger.
You have been saved uses the perfect tense, marking salvation as a completed action with continuing effect; the exclamation breaks into the sentence before the fuller statement in verse 8.
This not from yourselves most likely refers to the whole of salvation by grace through faith rather than to faith alone; either way the point is that salvation is entirely God's gift.
